questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: English-taught classes, and distance from home - Australia is very far away, so it felt like a good place to spend 6 months as it offered a basis from which to travel around that part of the world.

questions.answer: The information sent by UNSW ahead of my arrival was very comprehensive so I felt very prepared.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: They hosted a welcome event for all of the exchange students which went over the basics.  There is also an exchange society which we were told could help us if we needed - I did not use it but it is apparently quite helpful.

questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
No.  I found my first room through a friend at UCPH who is originally from Sydney.  One of her friends had a spare room.  However, that fell through as he asked me to leave so his friend could move in, so I used
flatmates.com.au
for my second apartment.  That also fell through a couple of weeks before I left as the couple had sold the apartment (without telling me), so I stayed in a hotel for my final weeks.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Make sure you sign a contract

How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Easy, once you understand the Moodle platform.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
1. You apply for approval to join the courses that you want.  This is additional to the KU pre-approval.  You can apply for approval of 3x as many classes as you can take (e.g. I could take 3 courses in Term 3, so I could apply for approval for 9).  Some of my applications were rejected as I did not meet the required criteria (e.g. some courses were reserved for people doing specific degrees).

2. Once you have been approved, you log into the portal (called Moodle) and can enrol in courses.  If the course is full, you can join the waitlist.  Once you have enrolled, you can change your mind up until 2 weeks into term. 

3. A few weeks after the course enrolment, you can register for lectures and classes (either online or in-person) depending on what times work for you.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: UNSW has the Nucleus in the library, which is open from 10am-5pm every weekday.  They could help you with pretty much anything relating to university, including registration for classes.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got into every class I wanted.  However, some of my friends were not as lucky, especially those taking papers with the law school as the classes were smaller.   I was very proactive in checking when course/class registration opens (at least twice a day).

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: You will not get a notification when registering for classes opens, so check the portal regularly, as classes fill up quickly.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
The reading was very challenging and, I felt, a higher standard and quantity than that assigned at UCPH.  The exams were usually in the form of essays (with a few online quizzes) and the essay questions were preset, and very challenging.  I felt like I learnt loads and I greatly enjoyed what we studied.

However (developed below), 374 of the 375 people in my class were from China - this is not a problem in itself, but very few of them spoke any English - I asked a few people what their names were, and they did not understand and asked me to ChatGPT it.  As a result, they did not participate in class at all.  If the teacher asked them a direct question, they would use ChatGPT (even playing the ChatGPT voice out loud to answer).  While in some ways this benefitted my learning, as I essentially had a one-to-one tutorial (as no one else was participating) every time, I think a very valuable part of a Masters’ Programme is learning from your peers, and I could not talk to them.  Further, the clear and constant use of AI both in class and during essay submissions made me doubt the integrity of the overall academic programme.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I did four courses, all at MA level (see below).  However, one class (LAWS8168) was combined with the BA version of that class (LAWS3368), so we learnt the same content.  But the MA students had to write a longer essay.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: My programme at UCPH did not involve any lectures - instead we had 2 classes a week.  However at UNSW, each class would have one lecture and one class.  The classwork would be based on the lecture, so attending the lecture was vital.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
1. The Australian Legal System in Comparative Perspective (LAWS3368)
2. The International Political Economy (POLS5122)
3. The Politics of International Law (POLS5125)
4. Development, Human Rights, and Global Health (COMD5002)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The International Political Economy (POLS5122) was excellent.  Very current, up-to-date, and interesting readings.  It examined the development of the existing global order and US hegemony after WWII, and how this impacts today’s politics, including Trump’s second term, the rise of China, tech billionaires, and global warming.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: While you have to pay 7,000 DKK for health insurance, the insurers will only usually pay out 50% of the total cost.  E.g. I had a routine medical exam for 900DKK, and only received 450DKK from the insurers.  I expected 100% of the fee to be paid, but apparently 50% is the usual policy.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Fresh produce (e.g. fruit/vegetables) and meat is much cheaper than Denmark, so food shopping was cheaper.  Healthcare is more expensive (see above).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
UNSW has very good sports clubs which train on campus.  They have different levels, so you can play at a high level or more casually.
UNSW hosted some aboriginal cultural events (such as Welcome to Country) which were very interesting and very .  There were societies (e.g. exchange societies) which hosted events such as hikes, drinks, socials.  
There are over 300 societies at UNSW covering pretty much everything.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I found that all of the societies/activities were geared towards undergraduates, so I did not participate much.  But, I did do Arc Sport, which is a casual practice/friendly games on Wednesdays in various sports.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: The Great Barrier Reef, Kakadu National Park, Uluru National Park, New Zealand

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I found it very easy as I am from the UK, which is a very similar culture to Australia.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I did not socialise with local students often, as no one in my class was Australian (see question 15 above and 44 below).  For general socialisation, join Facebook groups and go to events hosted by them, even if you do not know anyone.  Australians are very friendly so it is easy to join these sort of events.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Early morning culture (starting the day at 5am) took some getting used to.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Relaxed culture, friendly people, easy access to the beach, very stress-free culture.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Please see question 44 below about the biggest challenge. 
2. The workload is a lot higher than UCPH 
3. The marking is much harder than UCPH

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: No

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting new people and seeing new parts of the world.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The vast majority of postgraduate students enrolled at UNSW are from China.  My class had 375 students enrolled, and 374 of them were from China.  This is obviously not an issue in itself, but barely any of them spoke passable English and so did not participate in class; if they were asked a direct question by the teacher, they would rely on Google Translate or ChatGPT to answer.  While in some ways this benefitted my learning, as I essentially had a one-to-one tutorial (as no one else was participating), it was particularly limiting in terms of social life as I was unable to speak to my classmates without resorting to Google Translate.  It also limited employment opportunities, as I was told you cannot get a job on campus without knowledge of Mandarin.  Further, I think a very valuable part of a Masters’ Programme is learning from your peers, as well as the teacher, so being unable to communicate with my peers limited my experience both academically and socially.

questions.answer: Yes
